doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Declining students and his mother's teaching career
summary: He is shocked by his students' preparation, and tells how his mother returned to college and became a teacher; he blames the pace of life.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I am totally shocked. I had no idea that the level of intake — I mean these kids, they don’t know anything, I mean just compared to what it was — I mean just a rust belt, blue collar kid coming into a university had better speaking, writing, arithmetic skills, knew more about life, than any of these kids do. And now the best students are kind of similar to some of the best students, but it even becomes skewed with them because you can see certain little things that they don’t quite have that the best of the best students that you would see had. And that’s like whoa. Wait a minute. What has happened? And I’ve talked to my mother who retired as a middle school teacher. My mother is a great — I mean I’m not going to get into that too much but hell my mother raised six kids and she went to school and it broke her mother’s heart because she had me, she got married and had me at the end of the war instead of finishing her college education, as she was a year away. She went to a small black college, female college, Talladega College in Alabama and met my father and he swept her off her feet and I was born when she was 20 years old and all that kind of stuff. Anyway the point was that she had these six kids and she decided to go back to San Jose State after she’d been gone from college for 25 years raising kids. And they actually looked at her transcript and they said we’ll admit you as a second semester junior. And she said, “You will?” They said, “Yeah we’ll take your credits” and everything. So she wound up becoming a teacher and doing student teaching in the Monterey Peninsula School District and wound up becoming a teacher and then was there 20 years. She put in 20 years and she gets her retirement. So I mean I just look at that, and I’ve talked to her and I said what’s going on? She says, “Raymond that’s the way it is,” she says, “it’s unfortunate but the standards have just really—”
Does it have anything to do with attention spans do you believe?

I think attention span in part is produced because of the medias. I mean the media and the pace of our lives. I don’t think people — I don’t think it’s genetic or I don’t even think it’s really culturally induced, I think it’s just the pace that everybody has to now live a daily life is such that you don’t have time to actually have a longer view.
